slides.title: The meaning problem: numbers aren't meaning
slides.summary: Token IDs are just labels. To understand text, a machine needs two things IDs can't give it: what a word means, and what it means here.
body: After tokenizing, the model has a list of ID numbers. But an ID is only a label, like a locker number. Token 9246 could be "cat" and 9247 something completely unrelated. The numbers say nothing about meaning.

Computers can only do maths on numbers, and maths on labels makes no sense: "cat" + 1 isn't "kitten". <mark>The model needs to turn each token into numbers where similar meanings end up close together.</mark>

Even then, one word can mean different things: the bank of a river, or a bank that holds your money. Words like "it" and "they" point back to something said earlier. It's the same token ID every time, so the right meaning has to come from the surrounding words.

body.note: Two problems, two solutions. Embeddings give every token a meaning as a list of numbers (the next slides). Attention then adjusts that meaning to fit the words around it (the Attention chapter).

blocks.html: "carpet" sits right next to "cat" by number but means something unrelated, while "kitten" and "dog" are far away. The numbers carry no meaning. IDs are made up for illustration.

items.label: I paid the money into the bank.
The cat sat on the mat because it was warm.

blocks.html: Same ID, different meaning. Only the surrounding words can tell them apart.

items.label: Embeddings: meaning as numbers
items.sub: each token becomes a list of numbers; similar meanings sit close together

items.label: Attention: meaning in context
items.sub: each token updates its meaning using the words around it

blocks.html: Click either one to jump there.

slides.title: The embedding table
slides.summary: Each token ID picks one row of a big learned table. That row, a list of numbers, is the token's embedding.
body: A token ID is just a label: the number 8415 says nothing about meaning. So the model's first real step swaps each ID for a list of numbers, called a vector, by looking it up in an embedding table.

ul: One row per token. The table has a row for every entry in the vocabulary. Token 8415 ("␣cat") picks row 8415, and that row is its vector.
Thousands of numbers per row. Each row holds d numbers: 768 in GPT-2 small, 12,288 in GPT-3.
Almost free to run. It's a plain array lookup, with no maths at all.

body.note:
"I love Apple" → token IDs [40, 3021, 8325] → one row each:
40 → [0.12, 0.25, …]
3021 → [0.65, 0.10, …]
8325 → [−0.10, 0.90, …]
The IDs are GPT-4's real ones; the numbers are illustrative.

body.h: A starting point, not the final meaning

body: <mark>The looked-up vector is only the token's starting point: the table row stays fixed, while a copy of it flows through the model and gets updated with context.</mark>

Take Apple. It starts with the same vector in "I love Apple. I ate one this afternoon." and "I love Apple. They're launching new Macs this fall." As the model reads on, attention mixes in the surrounding words, and the context settles whether it's the fruit or the company.

body.more: Wait: the clue comes after "Apple". Can it still help?
text: In a chat LLM, each token can only read the words before it, so the vector for "Apple" never sees "ate one" or "Macs". Instead, the later tokens read both "Apple" and the clue, and the meaning is settled there. Embedding models, which read in both directions, do update "Apple" itself.
Capitalisation also helps a little: " apple" (token 24149) and " Apple" (token 8325) are different tokens with different rows.
body.link: How tokens read each other, in Attention

body: The numbers start out random. Training nudges them millions of times, and words used in similar sentences end up with similar rows. Unlike the fruit example in The big picture, no single number means "sweetness". Meaning is spread across all of them.

text: During training, together with everything else, not in a separate step first.
1. Before training: only the tokenizer is built. It fixes the vocabulary, and so how many rows the table has.
2. When training starts: every row is filled with small random numbers, so "cat" is no closer to "kitten" than to "carpet".

3. On every batch: the model predicts the next tokens and measures its mistakes, and backprop nudges all the weights, including the rows of the tokens in that batch. Common tokens get nudged constantly, rare ones less often.
4. After training: the table is frozen with the rest of the model.
Older NLP systems often did it the other way round: they trained word vectors first with tools like word2vec, then plugged them into a model. Modern LLMs learn them on the job.
body.link: How the nudging works, in Training

body: <mark>An embedding is a token's row in this table: a list of learned numbers, where similar meanings get similar numbers.</mark>

body.note: The table is learned along with the rest of the model, and in small models it's one of the biggest parts: GPT-2 small uses 38.6M of its 124M parameters here.

viz.html: Click a token to see which row it selects. GPT-2 small: 50,257 rows × 768 numbers ≈ 38.6M parameters in this one table.

figure.alt: The token space-cat has ID 8415. The ID picks row 8415 of the embedding table, which has one row per vocabulary entry. That row is a list of numbers, the token's vector: 768 numbers in GPT-2 small, 12,288 in GPT-3. After training, similar words have similar rows: cat and kitten have nearly the same pattern of numbers, while carpet looks completely different. The numbers shown are illustrative.
figure.caption: The ID picks a row; the row is the vector. After training, "cat" and "kitten" have nearly the same row, while "carpet" looks nothing like them.

slides.title: Who picks the size of a vector?
slides.summary: The number of dimensions is a design choice made before training. It sets the width of the whole model, and its cost grows with the square of the width.
body: Training learns the numbers in the embedding table, but not its shape. The people building the model choose d (also called d_model or hidden size) before training starts, and it never changes. The dimensions don't get assigned meanings either. Training decides what each one ends up encoding.

body.h: It's the width of the whole model

body: d isn't only the embedding size. Every token's vector keeps that size through every layer, so every attention and MLP layer is built to read and write d numbers. Choosing d means choosing how wide the entire model is.

ul: Pick a size. Teams decide how big the model will be from how much computing they can pay for. Research shows that size and training data matter much more than the model's exact shape.
Share it between width and depth. That size is spent on wider vectors (a bigger d) or more layers. Bigger models usually get more of both.
Round for the hardware. Widths are multiples of 64 or 128 so the maths fits GPU chips neatly. That's why you see 768, 4,096 and 12,288, but never 1,000.

body.text: Shape is how the parameters are arranged: how wide each vector is (d), how many layers there are, and how many attention heads each layer has. Two models of the same size but different shapes usually perform about the same, as long as neither is extremely wide or extremely deep. For example, 24 layers with vectors 1,856 numbers wide and 48 layers with vectors 1,312 numbers wide both come to about 1 billion parameters, and they end up almost equally good.

body: Wider vectors give the model more room to store meaning, but each layer's cost grows with d²: doubling the width makes every layer about four times bigger.

body.text: Every number going into a layer connects to every number coming out, and each connection is one weight. With d numbers in and d out, that's d × d weights. In the figure below, 8 neurons connect to the next 8 with 64 lines. Double them to 16 and you get 256 lines: 4× the weights for 2× the width. Each weight is used once for every token, so the computing grows with d² too. A transformer layer holds several of these grids, which adds up to about 12 × d² per layer.
body.link: Count them up in The transformer block

body.note: The width also sets the size of the KV cache, the memory a model keeps for every token in the conversation (see Output & inference). Wider and deeper models need more memory per user, which is a big part of what they cost to serve.

figure.alt: Two models with the same number of parameters but different shapes. Each is drawn as a small neural network, with circles for neurons and lines for weights. Model A is wide and shallow: few, tall columns of neurons, standing for 24 layers that are 1,856 numbers wide. Model B is narrow and deep: more, shorter columns, standing for 48 layers that are 1,312 numbers wide. Each comes to about 0.99 billion parameters, using 12 times d squared per layer. After training on the same data, both reach almost the same quality. In scaling-law studies (Kaplan et al., 2020), models of the same size with very different shapes ended up within a few percent of each other. Only extreme shapes hurt: for example 2 layers with d = 6,450 is also about 1 billion parameters, but has too few layers to build up meaning. Quality bars are illustrative.
figure.caption: Same budget, two shapes: 24 wide layers or 48 narrow ones, drawn as small neural networks. Trained on the same data, they end up almost equally good. Only extreme shapes fall behind.

blocks.html: Width and depth grow together. The width always splits evenly into attention heads (Attention chapter): d = heads × head size.

items.label: Wider: more room for meaning
items.sub: more concepts fit without crowding, and there's room for more attention heads

items.label: Wider: cost grows with d²
items.sub: 2× the width ≈ 4× the parameters and computing per layer, plus a bigger embedding table and KV cache

items.label: Too narrow: a bottleneck
items.sub: everything the model knows about a token has to squeeze into one vector, and extra layers can't fix that

items.label: Deeper instead: more steps
items.sub: more layers can build on each other, but they run one after another, which adds delay

blocks.html: No single best width exists. Labs pick a total size for their budget, then choose a sensible shape.
The table grows with d but the layers grow with d², so in big models the embedding table becomes a tiny share of the total.

slides.title: What the positions of vectors mean
slides.summary: After training, similar words sit close together, and some relationships point in a consistent direction.
body: If you could plot the trained vectors, you'd see a pattern. <mark>Words with related meanings group together: fruits near fruits, programming languages near programming languages.</mark>

Some relationships even become consistent directions. Going from "man" to "woman" points roughly the same way as going from "king" to "queen". That's why the famous sum king − man + woman ≈ queen roughly works, first shown with word2vec in 2013.
Why does this happen? Words that appear in similar sentences get nudged in similar ways during training. "Cat" and "kitten" both show up near "purr" and "pet", so their vectors drift together.
Closeness is measured with cosine similarity, the same calculation as the fruit comparison in The big picture.
<mark class="info">The table gives each token one fixed vector. "Bank" gets the same vector by a river and in the high street. Attention, in the next chapter, adjusts it to fit the sentence.</mark>

body.note: This is exactly how semantic search and RAG work. Turn every document into a vector once, turn the user's question into a vector, and return the documents whose vectors are closest. Vector databases exist to do this search quickly. Search uses a different kind of embedding, one vector for a whole text, which the next slide explains.

figure.alt: Three views of what trained embedding vectors look like, drawn in two dimensions. First, words with related meanings cluster: apple, mango, banana and cherry sit together; cat, kitten, dog and puppy sit together; Python, Rust, Java and Go sit together. Second, relationships become consistent directions: the arrow from man to woman points the same way as the arrow from king to queen, and the arrow from man to king matches woman to queen, so king minus man plus woman lands near queen. Third, closeness is measured by angle: cat and kitten point in almost the same direction, with cosine similarity about 0.97, while cat and carpet are far apart, about 0.11. Positions and numbers are illustrative.
figure.caption: Three patterns in trained embeddings: related words cluster, relationships like male → female point the same way, and closeness is measured by the angle between vectors.

viz.html: A 2D sketch. Real embeddings have hundreds to thousands of dimensions, and these neat directions are only roughly true.

slides.title: Token embeddings vs sentence embeddings
slides.summary: An LLM gives every token its own vector from a table. Search and RAG need one vector for a whole piece of text, made by a separate embedding model.
body: The word embedding is used for two different things, and they're easy to mix up.

body.h: Token embeddings: one vector per token

ul: A lookup. Each token ID picks its row from the embedding table on the previous slides.
No context. "Bank" gets the same vector by a river and in the high street. Context comes later, from attention.
Internal. They're the LLM's starting point. You rarely use them directly. To see what such vectors look like, try the Embedding Projector on the right.

body.h: Sentence embeddings: one vector per text

ul: Run the whole text through a model. An embedding model is a transformer, so attention mixes context into every token's vector.
Squash it into one vector. Average all the token vectors, or take the vector of one special token.
Trained for similarity. Training pulls together texts that mean the same thing, such as a question and its answer, and pushes unrelated texts apart.

body: <mark>A token embedding is a lookup at the start of an LLM. A sentence embedding is the output of a whole model, built so that texts with similar meanings get similar vectors.</mark>

body.more: Why not just average the token embeddings from the table?
text: It's cheap, but it loses too much. The table's vectors have no context, so the average can't tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog": same tokens, same average. It also can't tell a river bank from a money bank.

An embedding model runs attention first, so each token's vector already reflects the words around it before they're combined. That's also why embedding models are trained specially: a plain LLM's vectors aren't tuned for comparing texts.

body.note: This is what an embeddings API returns. OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small gives 1,536 numbers per text, and the open all-MiniLM-L6-v2 gives 384, however long the text is (up to the model's limit). You store these in a vector database and compare them with cosine similarity.

code: # token embeddings: one row per token, no context
# sentence embedding: run a model, then pool
h = encoder(ids)        # [n, d], context mixed in
v = h.mean(dim=0)       # [d], one vector for the text

figure.alt: Two kinds of embedding compared. First, token embeddings: the tokens The, cat and sat each look up their own row in the embedding table, giving three vectors, one per token. They carry no context, so the token cat gets exactly the same vector in every sentence. They are the LLM's input. Second, a sentence embedding: the whole text "The cat sat on the mat" goes through an embedding model, a transformer whose attention mixes context into every token. That gives six context-aware vectors, which are averaged into one vector for the whole text. That vector is compared with other texts by cosine similarity: "A cat was sitting on a rug" scores 0.91 and "Where did the cat sit?" 0.78, while "Stock prices fell today" scores 0.06. Sentence embeddings are used for search, RAG, clustering and recommendations. Vector values and scores are illustrative.
figure.caption: Token embeddings are looked up one per token. A sentence embedding runs the whole text through a model and averages the result into one vector, ready to compare with other texts.

viz.html: Both are lists of numbers where close means similar. The difference is what gets a vector, and whether context is included.

viz.title: See it in 3D: Embedding Projector
viz.description: Explore 10,000 word vectors squashed down to 3D. Search for a word such as "cat" to highlight its nearest neighbours. These are word2vec vectors, an older kind of word embedding rather than an LLM's own table, but they show the same idea: related words sit close together. It works best in a new tab, where its search box has room.

slides.title: Cosine similarity: comparing meaning
slides.summary: Cosine similarity scores how closely two vectors point the same way. It finds texts about the same thing, but can't tell whether they're true, safe or in agreement.
body: "How do I reset my password?" and "I'm locked out of my account. What should I do?" share few words and differ in length, yet ask the same thing. A good embedding model gives them vectors that point the same way.
Cosine similarity measures the angle between two vectors and ignores their length: 1 means same direction, 0 unrelated, and −1 opposite (rare with real text).
<mark>Cosine similarity compares direction, not length, so texts with the same intent score high even when their wording and length differ.</mark>

body.h: What a high score doesn't tell you

ul: Truth. "The Eiffel Tower is in Paris" and "…is in Rome" score high. A vector captures what a text is about, not whether it matches the world, so a false claim sits right next to the true one.

Agreement. "JavaScript is the best language" and "…the worst language" are both opinions about JavaScript. The topic dominates the vector, and the opinion is a small part of it, so opposite views land close together.

Negation. "This drug is safe" and "This drug is not safe" differ by one word. The vector is mostly built from content words like drug and safe, and few training pairs hinge on a single "not", so it barely moves.

Safety and quality. Harmful instructions sit next to harmless questions on the same topic, and a sloppy, wrong answer next to a careful one. Search returns them all; judging which is safe or good takes a separate step.

Relevance. Questions tend to look like other questions. "What causes rain?" can score higher against "What causes snow?" than against a paragraph that actually answers it. Search-tuned embedding models are trained on question-and-answer pairs to reduce this.

body: <mark>Embeddings capture relationships between texts. They don't check facts, intent, quality or safety.</mark>

text: Take the dot product, then divide by both vectors' lengths: cos = a · b / (|a| × |b|).
Dividing by the lengths removes size from the picture. [3, 4] and [6, 8] have lengths 5 and 10 but point the same way, so their cosine is exactly 1.
body.link: The basics with fruit vectors, in The big picture

text: Exact details blur. "Error 404" and "Error 500", or two product codes, look almost identical as vectors.
Long texts dilute. One vector for a 50-page document mixes many topics, so documents are split into chunks first.
Scores belong to one model. A 0.8 from one model isn't a 0.8 from another, and vectors from different models can't be compared at all.
Bias comes along. Embeddings learn from human text, stereotypes included. A 2016 study found word vectors linking "man" to "programmer" and "woman" to "homemaker".

body.note: Many embedding APIs, including OpenAI's, return vectors of length 1, so cosine similarity is just the dot product. Real RAG systems treat similarity as a fast first pass: hybrid search adds keyword matching, a reranker rescores the top hits, and the LLM plus safety checks judge what the text actually says.

code: q = embed("How do I reset my password?")

figure.alt: Cosine similarity compares the angle between two vectors, not their length. First, two vectors pointing the same way but with different lengths, a short question and a long, detailed version of it, have a cosine of 1. Second, two vectors at right angles have a cosine of 0: unrelated, nothing in common. Third, two vectors pointing in opposite directions have a cosine of minus 1, which is rare with real text. Fourth, the calculation: the dot product divided by both lengths. For a = [3, 4] with length 5 and b = [6, 8] with length 10, the dot product is 50, and 50 divided by 5 times 10 is 1: same direction despite different lengths. Below, a scale from minus 1 to 1 shows where real text pairs land: "How do I reset my password?" against "I forgot my password and I'm locked out of my account. What should I do?" scores 0.86, while "How do I reset my password?" against "What's the weather tomorrow?" scores 0.08. Scores are illustrative.
figure.caption: Same direction scores 1, at right angles 0 and opposite −1, whatever the lengths. That's why a short question and a long, detailed one can still match.

slides.title: Word order matters: adding position
slides.summary: Attention doesn't notice word order by itself, so position information has to be added.
body: Attention, the core step in the next chapter, compares every token with every other token. On its own it treats the input like a bag of words: shuffle the tokens and each one gets the same result. <mark>It can't tell "dog bites man" from "man bites dog".</mark>
So position has to be added in. The original Transformer (2017) added a fixed pattern of waves to each token's vector:

ul: Each pair of numbers goes up and down at a different speed, from very fast to very slow.
Together they give every position its own unique fingerprint.
Nearby positions get similar fingerprints, so the model can tell near from far.

body.note: Think of a clock with many hands. The second hand alone can't tell you the time. But seconds, minutes, hours and days together mark every moment uniquely, and moments close together look alike.

body: In the heatmap, each row is a position and each column is one number. The fast-changing columns are on the left and the slow ones on the right.

figure.alt: Why models need position, and how the original Transformer added it. First, without position, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" contain the same three tokens, so attention alone gives the same result for both. Second, with position, every token is stamped with its place in the sentence, 0, 1 or 2, so "dog at position 0" and "dog at position 2" become different inputs: the input is the token vector plus a position vector. Third, the position vector comes from waves at different speeds. Four waves are drawn across positions 0 to 16, from the fastest to the slowest. Reading all four waves at position 5 gives that position its own stamp: about −0.96, +0.60, +0.89 and +0.43. Nearby positions get similar stamps.
figure.caption: Without position, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" look the same to attention. A position vector, read off waves at different speeds, stamps each token with where it sits.

slides.title: RoPE: what modern models use
slides.summary: Modern models mark position by rotating vectors, so attention can directly see how far apart two tokens are.
body: Most current open models (Llama, Mistral, Qwen and others) use rotary position embeddings (RoPE) instead. Nothing is added to the token's vector. Instead, inside attention, the query and key vectors (next chapter) are rotated by an angle that grows with the token's position.

Why rotate? Attention scores two tokens with a dot product, and the dot product depends on the angle between the two vectors. Rotate one by position m and the other by position n, and the angle between them only depends on m − n: how far apart they are.
Try it: move both sliders by the same amount. Both arrows turn, but the angle between them, and so the score, doesn't change.

body.note: RoPE tells the model relative position ("three tokens back"), not absolute position ("token 1,207"). That suits language, where nearby words usually matter most. It's also one reason context windows can be made longer after training.

code: q, k = rope(q, m), rope(k, n)   # then q·k as usual

figure.alt: How rotary position embeddings, RoPE, mark position. First, the same vector is drawn at positions 0 to 4: at each position it is rotated by one more step, theta. Second, a query at position 5 is rotated 5 steps and a key at position 2 is rotated 2 steps, leaving an angle of 3 steps between them. Third, a query at position 9 and a key at position 6 are both rotated further, but the angle between them is again 3 steps. Because the dot product depends on that angle, the same distance between two tokens gives the same attention score, wherever they are in the text.
figure.caption: RoPE turns queries and keys by their position. Two tokens 3 apart always end up 3 steps apart in angle, so they get the same score wherever they are.

slides.title: The input is now a matrix
slides.summary: The input stage ends with one vector per token. This is the residual stream that every later layer reads and updates.
body: Put the steps together: split the text into tokens, look up each token's vector, and add position. The result is a matrix with one row per token and d columns: shape [n, d], or [B, n, d] for a batch.
This matrix is called the residual stream, and it's the star of the rest of the course.
<mark>Every token is now a row of numbers that carries its meaning and its position. Every later layer reads from this matrix and adds its own bit back.</mark>

body.note: The shape stays the same all the way through the model until the very end. That's why you can stack 32, 80 or 120 identical layers: each takes [B, n, d] in and gives [B, n, d] out.

body: Each coloured square on the right is one number. Real rows have thousands.

figure.alt: The text "The cat sat" is split into three tokens with IDs 791, 8415 and 7731. Each ID looks up its row in the embedding table, giving one vector per token. A position signal is added to each vector (or, in models using RoPE, applied later inside attention). The result is a matrix with one row per token and d columns, shape n by d. This is the residual stream that every later layer reads and updates. Vector values are illustrative.
figure.caption: Everything in this chapter in one picture: token IDs become vectors, position is added, and the result is the [n, d] matrix the rest of the model works on.
